provenance: Certainly, delivered to the Marquise de Pompadour, for her castle of Ménars, circa 1760 | Guy-Louis Duboucheron collection ; | Pierre Cornette de Saint Cyr, 4 November 1995, lot 52 ; | Private collection, Brussels; passed down through the family. | | In 1760, the Marquise de Pompadour acquired the Château de Ménars and wished to recreate within this 17th-century château the surroundings in which she lived at court. Ange-Jacques Gabriel contributed to the château by introducing a new style: Neoclassicism. The finest craftsmen were involved in this project, which was almost complete by the time of her death in 1764. | After her death, Ménars passed to her brother, the Marquis de Marigny, who retained it in its entirety whilst the other properties were sold. It is likely that the new style of Ménars appealed to him and that its modernity prevented him from selling it. | | The Marquise de Pompadour's refinement needs no introduction; she was always on the lookout for innovation. Her pervasive influence on the arts made her the woman who set trends. It was against this backdrop of renewal that she chose Neoclassicism for the new interior design of Ménars, breaking with the Rococo style she had once so loved. | | As for furnishings, she commissioned new furniture from Jean-François Oeben, with whom she developed a relationship of trust given the scale of her commissions. Thus, the inventory drawn up after JF Oeben's death in 1763 indicates that Madame de Pompadour had paid him, between 1761 and 1763, the considerable sum of 17,400 livres as a deposit for furniture to be supplied for her various residences. One of the most significant commissions was this exceptional set of seventeen chests of drawers known as "à la grecque", mostly made of mahogany, but also of satinwood and marquetry. | These chests of drawers, all constructed in the same manner, feature a central projection, three drawers in a band, and two large drawers flanked by two side panels; they are closed by one of the large drawers, which thus blocks all the openings. | Upon the death of Jean-François Oeben in 1763, the inventory still lists the following in his possession: « trente quatre madriers de bois d'acajou...par ordre et pour le compte de la dite dame marquise de Pompadour pour être employés à faire des meubles pour ces différentes maisons de la dite dame ». | We are currently aware of a number of chests of drawers of this model | Collection de Madame Evain, vente Paris, le 21 février 1945, lot 201 ; Palais Galliera, le 22 novembre 1982, lot 144 ; Maître Rouillac, vente Cheverny, 23 juin 1990, lot 416 ; vente Sotheby's Zurich le 10 décembre 1996, lot 448 ; Vente à Versailles, Mes Perrin et Royère, le 30 novembre 1997, lot 120 ; Christie's à Monaco le 28 avril 2000, lot 78 ; Sotheby's , 2009, le lot 81 ; Sotheby's, 2018, le lot 142 | une commode reproduite A. He and his wife, the Archduchess Maria Beatrice, visited Paris from 11 May 1786 until 18 August 1786, on which occasion they received the service. | | The service described as "fond bleu céleste, Marguerites barbeaux et Roses" in the sale records included 72 plates at 36 livres each. provenance: Anon. sale, Neumeister Munich, May 1974, lot 152; | Anon. sale, Christie's London, 8 July 2002, lot 2; | European Private Collection, sold at Bonhams London, 9 December 2021, lot 148 | | Literature | Kopplin, Monika et al., Schwartz Porcelain, 2003, no. 87, p. 180, ill. 20; | Guofan Hong (ed.), Meissen Porcelain: Three Hundred Years of "White Gold," 2023, no. 60 | | Exhibited | Münster, Museum für Lackkunst, Schwartz Porcelain, 7 December 2003-7 March 2004; | Schloss Favorite bei Rastatt, Schwartz Porcelain, 29 March-27 June 2004 | | In 1717, the Meissen manufactory administrator, Johann Melchior Steinbrück, recorded that by Easter 1710, Johann Friedrich Böttger had produced stoneware with a variety of decoration, including "...mit schwartzer Glasur überzogen, und also wieder eine ganz neüe Arth von porcelain, dergleichen man aus Indien noch keines gesehen [...] Dieses schwartzglasurte nun hat Er ferner zum Theil schneiden, daß man die rothe Substanz neben dem schwartzen sehen; theils auch mit Golde und Farben laquieren laßen; wodurch es ein sehr schönes Ansehen bekommen" [...covered with a black glaze, and so again a new type of porcelain, the like of which is not seen from India. He has also cut some of the black-glazed so that the red substance is visible alongside the black; some is also lacquered with gold and colours, which lends it a very beautiful appearance] (quoted by M. Cassidy-Geiger, "'Eine gantz Neue Arth von Porcellain' Die Produkte der Meißener Manufaktur im Stil von Lack," in Kopplin, Schwartz Porcelain, p. 141). Stoneware decorated in imitation of lacquer was first offered for sale at the Easter Fair in Leipzig in May 1710. | | Martin Schnell (1675-before 1740) was appointed "Hoflackierer" in Dresden at the beginning of 1710 and maintained a flourishing workshop there for 20 years. He was included by Böttger among the manufactory personnel lists in 1710 and 1711. In 1712, he is listed in first position with a high monthly salary of 100 Taler (twice that of Böttger and more than three times that of Michael Nehmitz, the manufactory director). He is not mentioned in the salary lists from 1716, probably because he was preoccupied with other commissions, notably the furniture and decoration of the palace acquired by Augustus the Strong in May 1717, which was later renamed the Japanese Palace. | | The 1770 inventory of the Japanese Palace included six such octagonal black-lacquered stoneware coffee pots under no. 52 - including two with silver mounts - along with a note that three were somewhat damaged (see Anette Loesch (ed.), "Sächsisch schwartz lacquirtes Porcelain", 2013, nos. A32-35, pp. 170f). None of these remain in the Dresden Porcelain Collection, though two (unmounted) examples, apparently without Japanese Palace inventory numbers, were sold from the Dresden Porcelain Collection in 1919 (Rudolph Lepke's Kunst-Auctions-Haus, Berlin, 7-8 October 1919), lots 56 (the cover lacking finial) and 57 (unillustrated).

Jahrhunderts, 1980, p. 47). | | Numerous examples of the shape (called "Glocken Thee Krügel" [bell teapot] are listed in the 1711 inventory of the manufactory (C. Boltz, "Formen des Böttgersteinzeugs im Jahre 1711," Mitteilungsblatt der Keramikfreunde der Schweiz, 96 (1982): 23), and three are listed in the inventory of the Japanese Palace under no. 149: "Drey Stück [Thee Potgen] runde geschliffene, different, mit Deckel, Henckel und Schnauze, wovon eins mit einem silbernen Kettel versehen, 4 1/2. Zoll Hoch, 3 1/2. Zoll in Diam: No. 149" [three (tea pots) round, polished, different, with cover, handle and spout, of which one is decorated with a silver chain] (quoted by C. Boltz, "Japanisches Palais-Inventar 1770 und Turmzimmer-Inventar 1769," Keramos 153 (1996): 106). The form was decorated in a variety of methods, sometimes in combination, including wheel-cut decoration, polishing, faceted and black-glazed; see C. Boltz, "Steinzeug und Porzellan der Böttgerperiode," Keramos, 167/168 (2000): p. 106.

An additional teabowl was sold at Christie's London, 5 July 2004, lot 13. Höroldt is recorded as having decorated a service in red as early as 1720 (Pietsch 1996, p. 38), though the present example can be dated to around 1723 thanks to the K.P.M. mark. Several pieces from the service including the present lot were exhibited in Dresden in 1996 (Pietsch 1996, nos. 7-12), when the decoration was attributed in part to Höroldt himself. A beaker and saucer and a teabowl and saucer are in the Carabelli Collection (U. Pietsch, Frühes Meissener Porzellan, 2000, nos. 2-3). provenance: The Pavlovsk Palace, The Grand Duke Michael Pavlovich (1798-1849) son of Tsar Paul I (1798-1801) and brother of Tsar Alexander I (1801-1825) and Tsar Nicholas I (1825-1855). |  | The monogram belongs to Grand Duke Michael Pavlovitch (1798–1849), the youngest son of Czar Paul I and Empress Maria Feodorovna, and the brother of Czars Alexander I and Nicholas I. He came to Paris in 1814 as part of the Allied forces and, upon returning to Russia, undertook extensive travels throughout the empire. Shortly thereafter, he was appointed Commander of the Guards' Infantry Brigade and played a key role in the establishment of the High School of Artillery in St. Petersburg. |  | Michael Pavlovitch later distinguished himself in the war against Turkey, for which he was awarded the Order of St. George. In 1831, he was entrusted with the oversight of all military schools in Russia, a position he held with notable dedication. He married his cousin, Princess Helen of Württemberg, and together they had six daughters. |  | Michael Pavlovitch and his brother, Tsar Nicholas I, were regular patrons of the leading Parisian silversmiths of their day, including Martin-Guillaume Biennais, Jean-Baptiste-Claude Odiot, and Jean-Charles Cahier. The extensive service produced by Cahier for the Pavlovsk Palace ultimately numbered more than one thousand pieces and was completed over the course of several years. In the period between the First and Second World Wars, the Soviet government dispersed part of the service, much of which later entered the renowned Taïgou collection. |  | <u>Pavlovsk Palace</u> | Pavlovsk Palace was chiefly built between 1782 and 1786 for Grand Duke Paul (1754–1801) and Maria Feodorovna (1759–1828) on land gifted by Catherine the Great to celebrate the birth of their first son, the future Emperor Alexander I. The interiors of Pavlovsk Palace were shaped by Charles Cameron's deep admiration for antique art and Palladian classicism, drawing on the geometric harmony and proportional systems associated with Andrea Palladio, whose original drawings Cameron encountered through the Burlington circle in England. Under Vincenzo Brenna, the palace's rooms adopted a more ceremonial neoclassical grandeur, enriched with classical decorative themes across suites such as the Throne Hall and Picture Gallery. Later contributions by Carlo Rossi, Giacomo Quarenghi, Andrey Voronikhin, and Pietro Gonzaga continued this classical lineage, blending Russian and European neoclassical traditions into a unified decorative whole.

description_block: Jean-Charles Cahier, Paris, 1819-1838 The circular base with a broad torus of leaves alternating with acanthus, on a matte ground and bordered by a beaded edge, the ombilicus chased with a band of darts, the upper section decorated with alternating palmettes and rings on a matte ground. The stem formed of large alternating darts, the upper section with pierced silhouettes in the manner of Thomire, the three arms issuing from a central element applied with four classical female masks, each arm decorated with palmettes, stars, and rings on a matte ground, the base of each arm with a large coiled ring terminating in a flower bud, the centre modelled as a dog's head. Engraved with crowned cypher 'MP' for Mikhail Pavlovich (1798 - 1849), maker's mark C.
